Research Overview

Author

Stephen Stretton

This research portfolio focuses on climate policy, climate finance, applied modelling, taxation, and sovereign incentives. The common thread is practical climate statecraft: making climate strategy operational for finance ministries, multilateral development banks, and country teams through better models, diagnostics, policy instruments, and financing structures.

1. Carbon Pricing: carbon pricing in open economies

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it charges for the carbon in what the economy consumes, so it falls on exports and spares imports. The series argues that production and consumption should be priced separately: production intensity with a revenue-neutral feebate, consumption with a destination-based charge through VAT and a forward obligation on fuel suppliers, and both measured on one carbon-price-equivalent scale (paper 6.1, in section 6). Paper 1.1 sets out the architecture; the others carry the detail. Each paper comes as a short policy brief in the Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs series and a longer working paper. Section overview → · Series slides →

1.1 Price Production and Consumption Separately

A two-track architecture for carbon pricing in open economies

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it makes consumers pay for the carbon they use. This paper separates the jobs. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity at no cost to the treasury and with a small price effect. A carbon component of VAT and forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers price consumption, imports included. A carbon-price-equivalent metric measures both. International payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a net gain, and destination-based charges turn leakage into a race to the top.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1) → · Working paper → · Slides →

1.2 Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill

Decarbonizing coal-heavy power and trade-exposed industry

Carbon taxes stall where coal dominates power or where industry competes abroad, because the tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit, not only for the tonnes they could avoid. A revenue-neutral feebate charges producers above a sector benchmark of emissions per unit of output and rebates those below it. It gives the same incentive to switch as a tax at the same rate but leaves average costs almost unchanged. Governments should use feebates where carbon taxes stall.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.2) → · Working paper → · Slides →

1.3 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

Carbon price recognition and scrap shuffling under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism cuts an importer’s charge by the carbon price the exporter has effectively paid, installation by installation. Two flaws follow. Instruments that send a full price signal but pay little net, such as feebates, rebated carbon taxes and energy subsidy reform, earn no credit. And exporters can ship scrap-based steel to the EU and blast-furnace steel elsewhere, cutting reported embodied carbon with no fall in emissions. Measuring the price signal at country-sector level fixes both.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.3) → · Working paper → · Slides →

1.4 Carbon Consumption Tax

A carbon component in VAT and a forward obligation on energy suppliers

The EU prices the carbon its factories and power plants emit but barely prices the carbon in what Europeans buy, much of it emitted abroad. A carbon component of VAT charges every good consumed in the EU, imported or domestic, for its embodied carbon while the value component of VAT falls; exports are zero-rated and imports start on generous, rebuttable default intensities. A legal obligation announced a decade ahead makes the few large suppliers of road and heating fuel pay for the carbon they sell.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.4) → · Working paper → · Slides →

2. Other Tax and Fiscal Policy: tax rent, not effort

Free movement of capital and people makes high tax rates on mobile income hard to sustain, so governments give up on high rates. The constraint binds only on the wrong base. Economic rent, from land that cannot move and market power earned from a country’s own customers, can be taxed heavily without driving anything away. Longer and older work on tax and fiscal reform, including the book Screwed?!, is under More papers and books. Section overview →

2.1 Taxing Rent, Not Effort

A simple design for land and corporate taxation consistent with free movement of capital and people

A tax design that reaches high effective rates on economic rent while keeping capital and people free to move: a reverse wealth tax on land, with an allowance below a threshold and a land value tax above it, and a corporate package that presumes large firms hold market power, taxing supernormal profits, mobile rent-bearing sectors and sales with deductions for genuine local presence.

Working paper →

3. Finance and Risk: making clean power an asset class

Clean power in developing countries is cheap to build and expensive to finance, because investors price risks the project cannot control. The series removes payment risk at its source with a payment intermediary, then turns projects into a few standard securities, each held by the investor who prices its risk most cheaply. Each paper comes as a short policy brief in the Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs series and a longer working paper. Section overview → · Series slides →

3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

A payment intermediary for clean power

Solar and wind plants are cheap to build in most developing countries but expensive to finance, because lenders price the risk that a state-owned distribution company will not pay for the power. This paper proposes a payment intermediary facility that buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time whatever the distributor does, and recovers arrears itself, behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance. In a stylized calibration the offtaker premium adds about 11 percent to the solar tariff; guaranteeing the contract removes all of it and saves about five dollars per dollar of the guarantor’s expected cost, while guaranteeing project debt saves less than it costs. India’s Solar Energy Corporation shows that the design works, and its distributors’ arrears show that it must come with utility reform. The state’s exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but it does not vanish.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.1) → · Working paper → · Slides →

3.2 From Projects to Asset Classes

Two-stage finance and synthetic sovereign bonds for clean power

Clean power projects in developing countries are financed one at a time, on bespoke terms, by investors who price construction, payment, currency and sovereign risk together. This paper splits each project at commissioning: development banks finance construction against a contingent purchase contract, and completed plants are pooled and refinanced through first-loss equity, a thin mezzanine and a senior synthetic sovereign bond co-guaranteed by highly rated sovereigns. A one-factor portfolio model shows that 5 to 10 percent subordination makes the senior bond near-AAA at plausible default correlations, and that refinancing cuts the levelized cost of solar power by about a quarter. Where there is no contract to guarantee, as for transmission, a tiered and conditional bond guarantee plays the same role.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.2) → · Working paper → · Slides →

4. Sovereign Incentives: reward governments, not projects

Cutting emissions pays off globally while the costs fall on national governments, so incentives for national climate policy must come from outside, and cash transfers on the needed scale are politically impossible. The series rewards governments with cheaper borrowing instead: a guarantee is worth the full spread to the borrower but costs its provider only expected loss, so on the development banks’ own sovereign loss record each dollar of donor cost delivers about 80 dollars of incentive. That record reflects the banks’ preferred-creditor status, which a new facility might not inherit, so the papers also report a stress case, in which each dollar delivers 2.7. Papers 4.1 and 4.2 are the flagships. Each paper comes as a short policy brief in the Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs series and a longer working paper. Section overview → · Series slides →

4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

Notional capitalized value and guarantee-based climate incentives

Climate finance pays countries for marginal emission cuts measured against counterfactuals nobody can observe, and pays almost nothing for carbon stocks never released. This paper proposes a notional capitalized value: a balance opened by a country’s carbon stock, debited for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance, and used not as cash but as guarantee capacity on the country’s green borrowing. Because a guarantee costs its provider only expected loss and the carry on a buffer, each dollar of donor cost delivers about 80 dollars of incentive on the development banks’ sovereign loss record, and 2.7 in a stress case. For a stylized forest country with Guyana’s carbon stock, a $5 billion balance saves $150 million a year and prices emissions at about $30 per tonne. Capacity that declines as clean technology costs fall is the cheapest way to make acting now beat waiting.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.1) → · Working paper → · Slides →

4.2 The Climate Investment Trust

Hold capital, lend its strength

Large international rewards for national climate policy fail because donors will not vote for cash transfers on the needed scale and governments cannot borrow against promised payments. This paper proposes a Climate Investment Trust that holds donor capital rather than spending it, and uses one pool three ways: as second-loss cover behind the guarantees that reward policy, as fee-earning co-investment in clean energy and regional first-loss funds, and as national beneficiary accounts that countries pledge as collateral now and draw only after 2050. On the development banks’ loss record each donor dollar held delivers about 80 dollars of interest savings; in a stress case where the Trust lacks their preferred-creditor status, $5 billion supports about $54 billion of guarantees and delivers 2.7 dollars per dollar.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.2) → · Working paper → · Slides →

4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

Standard indicators, verification and pricing

Sustainability-linked loans and bonds tie a government’s interest rate to climate indicators, but they remain rare, bespoke and small: Uruguay’s 2023 World Bank loan, the leading example, can save the country at most $12.5 million. This paper proposes standard indicators measured as outturns, baselines set by rule, verification from published data and a published pricing schedule, with a fixed coupon for investors and the performance reward paid by a trusted intermediary. Because an interest rebate is bounded by the interest bill, the main reward should be guarantee capacity or collateral, which delivers about 80 dollars of incentive per dollar of funder cost on the development banks’ loss record, and 2.7 in a stress case.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.3) → · Working paper → · Slides →

5. Modelling: models a finance ministry can audit

Ministries set carbon prices and sequence subsidy reforms with the help of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built by the World Bank and the IMF for more than 180 countries, but until 2026 almost nobody could check its numbers. This series is the paper-length companion to the open CPAT-AI project. It states the model’s method on a few pages, describes how it was rebuilt twice and what the rebuild found (228 bugs, 24 of them high priority), gathers its validation, and checks its price elasticities against the evidence; the extensions ministries ask for are the modular upgrades of section 6. The rule throughout: a model a ministry can use must be small enough to state, built twice, tested against data and other models, and extended only where policy needs it. Country results are illustrative tool output, not official estimates. Section overview → · Series slides →

5.1 The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief

How a finance-ministry climate model turns prices into fuel use, power investment, emissions and revenue

CPAT’s mitigation documentation runs to 57,000 words and disagrees with the model in places. This paper states the module’s method in one place, from the rebuilt and tested version, in about eighteen equations: retail prices built up from supply cost, taxes, subsidies and the carbon charge; fuel use responding through income, usage and efficiency elasticities; an engineering power model that dispatches, retires and invests at default costs of capital of 7.5 to 15 percent; emissions and revenue by accounting identities; and GDP moved a year later by fiscal multipliers. A worked example shows why a $50 carbon price cuts industrial coal by a third and road fuel by about 6 percent. The paper gives the corrected equation wherever the documentation is wrong and proposes a penalty-based alternative to the logit investment rule.

Working paper → · Slides →

5.2 CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool

What two AI-assisted rebuilds of CPAT found, and how policy models should be maintained

Legacy CPAT is a 21-megabyte workbook too large to audit cell by cell. In October 2026 it was rebuilt twice, with AI coding agents (Claude Code and GitHub Copilot) doing most of the construction: once as a readable Excel workbook written by code, once as a Python model that reproduces it to nine significant figures. One rule governed both: bugs are fixed and never copied; questionable but intended choices are copied and tracked. The rebuild registered 228 legacy bugs, 24 of high priority, plus 135 issues and 20 errors in the documentation, and writing the model a second time found seven bugs in the first rebuild. The lesson for ministries: specify a model by shared variable codes, build it twice, and test every release.

Working paper → · Slides →

5.3 Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons

What the published checks show, where the tool fits and where it does not

This paper gathers CPAT’s scattered validation and separates four tests: fit to the base year, back-casts against history, comparison with other models, and replication in independent code. The model fits its base year by calibration, tracks emission trends in back-casts from 2000 for Australia and the United States, misses China badly, and gives baselines and carbon-price responses of the same order as the IEA, Enerdata and the World Bank’s power planning model. Results move most with the price elasticities: a $75 carbon tax cuts G20 emissions by 29 percent at the defaults and by 7 to 39 percent across their plausible range. Every published check predates the bug fixes, so the paper sets out how to rerun them as part of the model’s test suite.

Working paper → · Slides →

5.4 Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?

A check against the evidence

Price elasticities set the size of every emission cut CPAT reports. This paper checks its default long-run elasticities, fuel by fuel and sector by sector, against published meta-analyses and reviews. Seven of ten fuel-sector pairs lie within the published range; diesel in industry, gasoline in services and electricity in services are too high, and road gasoline is double the estimate corrected for publication bias. Two structural choices matter more than any single value: CPAT applies the full long-run response within one year, overstating five-year responses by about half, and it has no cross-price terms, so there is almost no fuel switching outside power. The paper sets out a validation protocol for future updates.

Working paper → · Slides →

6. Modular Upgrades: extending the model where policy needs it

A model a ministry can audit has to stay small, and the questions ministries ask keep growing. The papers in this section add capability to CPAT as separate modules, each of which reads the model’s prices, fuel use and emissions, adds one piece of economics and states its method in a few equations: one carbon-price scale for any policy mix, exporters’ exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment, the cost of the clean capital and whether the budget should pay for it, one activity layer for linked models, and the path from a climate program to growth, revenue and debt. Country results are illustrative tool output, not official estimates. Section overview →

6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

The Total Effective Carbon Price: one carbon-tax equivalent for any mix of taxes, subsidies and standards

Countries cut emissions with taxes, subsidies, standards and mandates, yet standard metrics add up explicit prices per tonne, so a clean-fuel standard or a revenue-neutral feebate scores zero. The Total Effective Carbon Price is the single economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as the actual policy mix, with each instrument weighted by how strongly emissions respond. Crediting, border recognition and country diagnostics can all use it.

Policy brief (Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.1) → · Working paper → · Slides →

6.2 The CBAM Policy Tool

Measuring exporters’ exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment and what domestic policy can do about it

Since January 2026, EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity owe a carbon charge on embedded emissions. This paper describes a spreadsheet tool that computes the exposure product by product and year by year, and shows how verified emissions data, a domestic carbon price and rebates change it. At €80 per tonne, Turkish hot-rolled steel declared at the default owes €107 a tonne in 2026 and €252 at full phase-in, close to half its export price. The tool’s Egypt application shows why data matter most where a country has no default of its own: verified data would cut the full-phase-in charge on seven Egyptian exports from about €595 million to €177 million a year (illustrative tool results).

Working paper → · Slides →

6.3 Public Investment in CPAT

Investment needs and the efficiency of public spending

Carbon-pricing models say what a policy raises and cuts, but not what its clean capital costs or whether the budget should pay. This paper extends CPAT to price investment needs at the cost of capital countries actually face, and to test each use of public money against the cost of raising tax. A stylized clean asset fails the financial test above a 12.6 percent cost of capital, almost exactly CPAT’s default for lower-middle-income countries. In a stylized island, a solar plant worth $108 million fails the budget on a seven-year loan; concessional finance or a guaranteed power purchase agreement rescues it. Country runs put 2030 investment needs in Kenya, Uganda and St Lucia at 4 to 5 percent of GDP (illustrative tool results).

Working paper → · Slides →

6.4 Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT

One driver layer so four climate models can be linked

Four models used for climate-fiscal work build activity levels in incompatible ways: CPAT from GDP and prices, SISEPUEDE from income and population without prices, a border-adjustment tool from growth forecasts, and the Future Technology Transformations models not at all. This paper maps them onto ten common activities and sets out one constant-elasticity rule driven by population, income per person and the cost of the energy service, so the four can be linked on one baseline without counting a price response twice. Three propositions cover the population term, double counting and the vehicle chain. Under stylized growth, cars in use grow 64 percent in ten years while travel grows 41 percent.

Working paper → · Slides →

6.5 The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool

Linking energy investment and carbon pricing to growth, revenue and debt in one workbook

A ministry weighing a climate investment program needs its budget cost, what carbon pricing could pay for, and what both do to growth and debt, usually from separate teams. This tool chains them in one workbook for 186 countries: investment needs split by who pays, a screen for the most abatement carbon pricing can deliver within limits on political cost, open simplified versions of three IMF and World Bank macro-fiscal models, and a debt test. In a stylized run, financing and the efficiency of public investment move the result more than the program’s size. A run for Kenya finds a budget need of 0.5 percent of GDP in 2030, mostly land use and non-CO₂ spending; feasible power-sector pricing covers about 5 percent of it (illustrative tool results).

Working paper → · Slides →

7. Additional Analytics: diagnostics on data ministries already hold

Analysis changes policy only when the ministry that holds the budget can reproduce it. Each tool in this section takes data a finance ministry already holds or can download, puts it on a common scale and returns something sequenced enough to act on, built to one standard: every intermediate step visible, defaults defended line by line, and AI drafting checked against the source. The tools feed the other series: checked tax rates and externality values for CPAT and the carbon-pricing papers, and the cost-of-capital and incentive arguments carried into a country’s budget and debt. The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool, built to the same standard, extends CPAT and is paper 6.5 in section 6. Section overview → · Series slides →

7.1 The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic

Reading an excise system against its externalities

Excise schedules grow line by line for decades until nobody can read them whole, and few ministries can say whether their fuel, tobacco or alcohol taxes are high or low against the damage those goods do. The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic is a light, repeatable report that maps every line onto 30 standard lines, scales each rate three ways (US dollars per unit, share of price, revenue as a share of GDP), and sets fuel rates against a corrective benchmark built from one fixed set of values for carbon, air pollution, accidents, congestion and road damage. An AI model drafts each stage and every line is checked against the legal text. Run on the 2026 excise law of Sierra Leone and Liberia, it finds excise revenue of about 1.3 and 0.4 percent of GDP against an African average of 2.4: Sierra Leone taxes petrol at $0.23 a liter on a large fuel base, while Liberia taxes fuel only through levies of $0.095 a liter, below the cost of carbon alone, and books no excise on imported tobacco (illustrative results from the diagnostic, not official estimates).

Working paper → · Slides →

7.2 A Global Fiscal Indicators Dashboard for Climate-Fiscal Analysis

Eighty public indicators, one country profile, and a build anyone can rerun

Before advising on carbon pricing, subsidy reform or climate investment, an analyst needs a quick, comparable view of a country’s fiscal space, spending capacity, cost of capital and fossil fuel exposure. The dashboard assembles 80 indicators in twelve blocks for 217 economies from about twenty public datasets, scores them on one 1-to-10 scale and shows a one-page profile. A scripted pipeline rebuilds everything from the raw files, never imputes, records the year and source of every value, and stops if its configuration and outputs disagree. A comparison of four middle-income economies shows how the profile separates Indonesia’s revenue problem from South Africa’s debt-service problem.

Working paper → · Slides →

More papers and books

Work outside the seven sections: three books, papers on climate finance retained from earlier rounds, and essays written outside the professional portfolio. These are drafts kept as they stand rather than revised to the series standard. Overview of these papers →

Books

Time and Chance: The Elements of Scale in the Green Transition asks why clean energy costs too much in the countries that need it most, and works from the price of money through contracts and instruments to the institutions that would carry them. The Right Policy at the Wrong Time: Carbon Pricing and the Order of Things argues that the case for a carbon price was won intellectually and lost operationally, and makes the case for feebates and for sequencing. Sections 1, 3 and 4 hold the paper-length versions of several chapters; the overview places the two books against each other and against the papers. Screwed?! Getting Our Future Back with Tax and Benefit Reform (with Gordon Styles, 2020 manuscript) makes the case for reforming UK taxes and benefits, from tax principles, welfare and work to corporations, land, money and the environment.

Sustainability-Linked Intermediated Debt Instruments (SLIDIs)

With Marcello Estevão and Nils Zimmermann

A proposal to lower developing countries’ cost of borrowing while rewarding their governments for agreed environmental, social and governance progress, through sustainability-linked debt issued via an intermediary.

Paper →

The Sollar

A claim on installed solar capacity

One Sollar is an undivided share in a global portfolio of utility-scale solar parks, with net electricity revenue reinvested in more panels. Developers can borrow Sollars during construction and repay by issuing them against the finished park, financing the asset with a claim on what it will produce rather than with debt. The paper sets out the design and what it does not solve.

Paper →

Reforming MDBs

The role of the multilateral development banks in the green transition

The roles the multilateral development banks, and the World Bank Group in particular, could take in scaling climate action, as lenders and as policy influencers, and the two issues they must solve: scale and incentives for policy.

Paper →

Philosophy essays

Three essays on what happens when a governing metaphor stops being noticed as a metaphor. Order Without Ordinance is a dialogue on the picture of nature as law-governed, with an Indian case. The Politics of Life-Logic reads Nietzsche’s critique of Platonic governance alongside Chinese and Indian traditions and ends in proposals for reforming the World Bank. The Vocative Case asks what contemporary atheism is arguing with, and whether religious language was ever the kind of claim that can be refuted.

Overview → · Order Without Ordinance → · The Politics of Life-Logic → · The Vocative Case →

Political writing

Three pieces written outside the professional portfolio, not offered as research. Manifesto for a New American Republic is a short political statement on defending and then reforming the American constitutional order. Progressive Collapse of a Uniform Column derives the physics of a falling upper block from first principles, applies it to the World Trade Center towers and reports the gap between the model and the observed accelerations, without going further. Statistical Anomalies, Voting Machines, and the 2024 US Presidential Election assesses the statistical claims made about the election and concludes that the anomalies justify better data and audits, not the inferences drawn from them.
